titles.255: Annotatio IV §.II open: Internal obstacles — fountains from will’s pravity and intellect’s error; many rivulets
titles.256: Annotatio IV §.II: First fountain — free-acting pravity of will precedes intellect-error; sacred strife by free choice
titles.257: Annotatio IV §.II (1): Ambition / pride of life — hostile to truth and peace; Arius couplet
titles.258: Annotatio IV §.II (2): Lust of the eyes — excessive sacred curiosity; multiplies dogmas and unhealthy novelties
titles.259: Annotatio IV §.II (3): Lust of the flesh — φιλαργυρία with φιλαυτία; alien to Christian teachers

latin.255:
§. II.
Posteriores, Fontes dixeris alios, ex primis Actionum humanarum Principiis, Intellectui & Voluntati inhaerentibus vitiis communibus duobus, Pravitate & Errore exoriturus; alios Rivulos, ex fontibus memoratis scaturientes, eosque numero plures.
latin.256: Fontium binorum Priorem, Pravitatem Voluntatis facio-liberam, non minus sub Foedere Gratiae, quam Operum, errorem Intellectûs praevertentem: cum vel ipsius Foederis divini cujuscunque cum homine initi natura, tantum Luminis in intellectu humano supponat, quantum sufficit Pravitati voluntatis malitiosae vel cohibendae, vel repellendae, ut sic ad rixas sacras & dissidia Ecclesiastica praeter necessitatem, etiamsi instigante Diabolo, progressus, sciat, se non invitum, vel per errorem intellectûs, vel per Diaboli persuasionem, sed per liberam potius electionem suam ac προαίρεσιν, ad eandem provolâsse, promoventibus dissidiorum negotium rivulis majoribus tribus ex pravitate Voluntatis emanantibus & Johanni Apostolo probè notatis, hôc locô, inverso ordine recensendis:
latin.257:
Scilicet (1.) Fastu vitae, seu ambitione, sacro etiam ordini ut plurimùm adhaerente (uti constat in Pharisaeis Matth. 23, 5, 6, 7.) Veritati ac Paci perquam infesto Joh. 5, 44. & 7, 18. rixarum verò feracissimo 2. Tim. 3, 1, 2, 3. Ut vel ex vulgato isto, in Arrium rixatorem dicto, patet:
Quaeritur Haereticus (Schismaticus,) quare sit factus Arius,
In promptu Causa est, ambitiosus erat.
latin.258: (2.) Cupiditate oculorum, intellige Spiritualium, seu animae, verbô unô, Curiositate in Sacris nimiâ, ex ambitione ortâ, contra istud Apostoli ad Rom. 12, 3. μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν παρ’ ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν ἀλλὰ φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν (nam inflatus languet circa quaestiones. 1. Tim. 6, 3. 4. 5. Episcopo fugiendas, 2. Tim. 2, 23. 24. Tit. III. 9.), duo admodum mala, Paci Ecclesiasticae quam maximè infensa, progeneratura, dogmatum scil. Theologicorum multiplicationem eximiam; & noviter inventorum malesanam deperitionem.
latin.259: (3.) Cupiditate Carnis i. e. rerum Carnalium & mundanarum, unâ φιλαργυρίας vitiositate ab Apostolo redargutâ, quam Pharisaeis falsisque Doctoribus propriam Luc. 16. v. 14., & cum φιλαυτίᾳ cohaerentem. 2. Timoth. 3, 2, à Christianis Doctoribus alienam cupit Petrus 1. Pet. 5, 2.
latin.260: Posterior Fons, Error Intellectus est, quem pronus incurrit, quisquis voluntatis pravitati habenas laxat, sicuti vice versa, malitiam detestatus, veritati propior imminet. PS. 25. v. 14. Matt. 5. v. 8. Joh. 7. v. 17. Subnascitur autem error proximè ex praejudiciis, affectuum praedominio etiam educatione & informatione perversis, lectione librorum calumniosorum, hisque similibus;
latin.261: Perficitur vel malè & aegrè apprehendendo res Theologicas, adque amussim rerum terrestrium dijudicando, cum Nicodemo Joh. 3, 12. & Capernaitis Joh. 6. vel perversè componendo & apparenter contradictoria, extra Scripturam, conciliando. e. g. effata Christi duo Matt. 26. v. 11. & 28. v. 20. confictione duplicis Corporis Christi, visibilis & invisibilis, concilianda a. quàm facillimè distinctione Biblica inter duplicem Christi naturam, tàm Paulo Rom. 1. v. 3. 4. & Cap. 9. 5. quàm Petro 1. C. 3. v. 18. & Cap. 4. 1. recepta. Vel Confundendo diversa nec satis distinguendo, e. g. inter Veritates Theologicas quascunque, & inter Fundamentales magisque necessarias; vel Colligendo ineptè, e. g. negari omnipotentiam Divinam, dum de Dei voluntate & Revelatione in Dogmatibus quibusdam ambigitur; item, dissentientem omnia pro veris certisque habere, quae vel rectè, vel malè, ex Sententia ejus colliguntur. &c.

pass_a.255: §. II. The latter [obstacles], you may call other Fountains, arising from the first Principles of human Actions — two common vices inhering in Intellect and Will, Pravity and Error; other Rivulets springing from the fountains named, and those more in number.
pass_a.256: Of the two Fountains, the Prior is the free-acting Pravity of Will, which no less under the Covenant of Grace than of Works precedes the error of Intellect: since even the nature of any divine Covenant begun with man presupposes so much Light in the human intellect as suffices for the malicious Pravity of will either to be restrained or repelled, so that one who has advanced to sacred quarrels and Ecclesiastical dissensions beyond necessity, even with the Devil instigating, may know that he has rushed into the same not unwillingly, or through intellect’s error, or through the Devil’s persuasion, but rather through his own free election and προαίρεσις — three greater rivulets promoting the business of dissensions, flowing from the will’s pravity and well noted by the Apostle John, being here to be recounted in inverse order:
pass_a.258: (2.) By lust of the eyes — understand spiritual lusts, or of the soul; in one word, excessive Curiosity in Sacred things, sprung from ambition, against that word of the Apostle in Rom. 12:3, not to think beyond what one ought to think, but to think unto sobriety (for the inflated man languishes about questions — 1 Tim. 6:3–5 — which a Bishop must flee, 2 Tim. 2:23–24; Titus 3:9), about to breed two evils most hostile to Ecclesiastical Peace: namely an extraordinary multiplication of Theological dogmas; and an unhealthy doting on things newly invented.
pass_a.259: (3.) By lust of the Flesh, i.e. of carnal and worldly things, together with the viciousness of φιλαργυρία reproved by the Apostle, proper to Pharisees and false Teachers (Luke 16:14), and cohering with φιλαυτία (2 Tim. 3:2), which Peter wants alien to Christian Teachers (1 Pet. 5:2).
pass_a.260: The Posterior Fountain is Error of Intellect, which whoever loosens the reins to the will’s pravity is prone to incur — just as, conversely, one who detests malice draws nearer to the truth (Ps. 25:14; Matt. 5:8; John 7:17). But error is born proximately from prejudices, the predominance of affections, also perverse education and information, reading of calumnious books, and the like;
pass_a.261: It is perfected either by badly and weakly apprehending Theological things and judging them by the standard of earthly things, with Nicodemus (John 3:12) and the Capernaites (John 6); or by perversely composing and reconciling apparent contradictions outside Scripture — e.g. Christ’s two sayings Matt. 26:11 & 28:20, to be reconciled by inventing a double Body of Christ, visible and invisible, though far more easily by the Biblical distinction between Christ’s two natures, received both by Paul (Rom. 1:3–4; 9:5) and by Peter (1 Pet. 3:18; 4:1). Or by confusing distinct things and not distinguishing enough — e.g. between Theological truths of every sort and the Fundamental and more necessary ones; or by inferring ineptly — e.g. that Divine omnipotence is denied when God’s will and Revelation in certain Dogmas is debated; likewise, that a dissenter holds as true and certain everything rightly or wrongly inferred from his Opinion; etc.

255: §. II. The later obstacles you may call other fountains — arising from two common vices in the first principles of human action, intellect and will: pravity and error.
From those fountains spring still more rivulets, greater in number.
256: Of the two fountains, the first is the free-acting pravity of the will — which, under the covenant of grace no less than of works, runs ahead of intellect’s error.
For any divine covenant with man presupposes enough light in the mind to restrain or repel malicious will-pravity.

So whoever has gone on to needless sacred quarrels and church splits — even with the Devil prodding — should know he rushed in not unwillingly, nor merely by intellect’s mistake or the Devil’s talk, but by his own free choice and προαίρεσις.
Three larger rivulets from will-pravity, well marked by the Apostle John, promote that work of dissension; we list them here in reverse order:
257: (1.) Pride of life — or ambition — which usually clings even to the sacred order (as in the Pharisees, Matt. 23:5–7).
It is most hostile to truth and peace (John 5:44; 7:18) and most fertile of quarrels (2 Tim. 3:1–3).
That common couplet on quarrelsome Arius makes the same point: ask why the heretic (schismatic) Arius became what he was — the ready answer is, he was ambitious.
258: (2.) Lust of the eyes — meaning spiritual lusts of the soul; in a word, excessive curiosity in sacred things, born of ambition — against Romans 12:3: do not think beyond what you ought, but think unto sobriety.
For the puffed-up man languishes among questions (1 Tim. 6:3–5) that a bishop must flee (2 Tim. 2:23–24; Titus 3:9).
This breeds two evils most hostile to church peace: an extraordinary multiplication of theological dogmas, and an unhealthy doting on novelties.
259: (3.) Lust of the flesh — craving carnal and worldly goods — plus the love-of-money the Apostle rebukes as the mark of Pharisees and false teachers (Luke 16:14).
It sticks close to self-love (φιλαυτία, 2 Tim. 3:2), which Peter insists Christian teachers must keep far from (1 Pet. 5:2).
260: The second fountain is error of intellect — which anyone who loosens the reins to will-pravity is apt to fall into; conversely, whoever hates malice draws nearer the truth (Ps. 25:14; Matt. 5:8; John 7:17).
Error is born nearby from prejudices, passions in the saddle, warped schooling and teaching, the reading of slanderous books, and the like.
261: It is finished either by grasping theological things badly and weakly and measuring them by earthly standards — with Nicodemus (John 3:12) and the Capernaites (John 6) —

or by twisting apparent contradictions into harmony outside Scripture: for example Christ’s two sayings in Matt. 26:11 and 28:20, reconciled by inventing a double body of Christ, visible and invisible, though the biblical distinction of Christ’s two natures (Paul, Rom. 1:3–4; 9:5; Peter, 1 Pet. 3:18; 4:1) does it far more easily.
Or by confusing what differs and not distinguishing enough — e.g. any theological truths whatever versus the fundamental and more necessary ones;

or by inferring clumsily — e.g. that God’s omnipotence is denied when his will and revelation in some dogmas are debated; or that a dissenter holds as sure everything rightly or wrongly drawn from his opinion; and so on.
Stop before §. III (further rivulets from either fountain, noted by our Author).
